title: Text pipelines
summary: grep, cut, sort, uniq, wc, sed and awk: small tools that combine into answers.

steps.title: grep: lines that match
body: `grep PATTERN file` prints lines matching a **regular expression**.
| `-c` | count matching lines instead of printing |
Regex essentials: `^` start of line, `$` end, `.` any char, `*` zero or more, `[0-9]` a digit, `\b` word boundary.
grep -c " 500 " access.log           # how many server errors?
grep -rn "TODO" src/                  # every TODO with file:line
grep -Ev "^#|^$" sshd_config          # config without comments and blank lines

steps.prompt: Count the lines in `app.log` that contain `error`, `Error` or `ERROR`.
steps.explain: `-i` ignores case and `-c` counts. Order of flags doesn't matter (`grep -ic` works too).

steps.prompt: Which grep shows only the **uncommented, non-blank** lines of a config file?
steps.explain: `-v` inverts a pattern matching comment lines (`^#`) or empty lines (`^$`). Option 3 would also drop lines with a `#` in the middle, like `url=http://x/#a`.

steps.title: cut, sort, uniq, wc
body: sort file                     # alphabetical;  -n numeric, -r reverse, -k2 by field 2, -u unique
uniq                          # collapses ADJACENT duplicates; -c prefixes counts
**uniq only sees neighbours**, so you almost always `sort` first. The most famous pipeline in operations:
cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

steps.explain: Without `sort`, uniq only merges *adjacent* duplicates. Real uniq pads counts to 7 characters.

steps.prompt: Arrange the pipeline: the 3 most common HTTP status codes (field 9) in `access.log`, most common first.
steps.explain: Extract the field, group identical values together, count, sort by the count, take the top.

steps.title: sed and awk, just enough
body: **sed** edits a stream line by line. 90% of real use is substitution:
sed 's/http:/https:/' file        # first match on each line
sed -i 's/DEBUG/INFO/' app.conf   # edit the file in place
**awk** splits each line into fields `$1 $2 ...` (on whitespace by default) and runs a little program:
awk '{sum += $10} END {print sum}' access.log   # total bytes served

steps.explain: Fields are split on whitespace: $1=GET, $3=200. awk does arithmetic on numeric-looking fields.

steps.prompt: Match the job to the tool.
pairs: Replace every `localhost` with `db` in a file

steps.title: Count things with wc
prompt: The shop's logs are on your machine in `~/logs` (read `~/logs/README.txt` first). Answer with commands, writing **just the number** into each file under `~/answers/` (create it: `mkdir -p ~/answers`):
1. `requests.txt`: how many requests `access.log` holds (one per line).

checks.name: requests.txt is the number of requests
checks.fail: `~/answers/requests.txt` does not start with the number of lines in `access.log`.

checks.name: archived.txt is the number of archived logs
checks.fail: `~/answers/archived.txt` does not hold the number of files in `~/logs/archive`.

checks.name: words.txt is the number of words in README.txt
checks.fail: `~/answers/words.txt` does not hold the word count of `README.txt`.

hints: `wc -l file` counts lines, `wc -w` words. `wc -l < file` prints just the number, without the file name.
`ls dir` prints one name per line when it writes into a pipe, so `ls ~/logs/archive | wc -l` counts files.
`wc -l < ~/logs/access.log > ~/answers/requests.txt`, and the same shape for the other two.
steps.explain: `wc -l` is the quickest health check there is: how many requests, errors, files, users. Reading from `<` instead of naming the file makes it print only the number, ready to use in a script.

steps.title: grep -c, -i and -v (and rg)
prompt: Still on the logs in `~/logs`. Write each answer into `~/answers/`:
1. `errors.txt`: how many lines of `app.log` mention **error** in any capitalisation (`ERROR`, `Error`, `error`).
2. `not-health.txt`: how many requests in `access.log` are **not** health checks (`/healthz`).
3. `timeouts.log`: the lines themselves (not a count) of `app.log` that mention **timeout** in any case but **not** `retrying`.
4. `oom.txt`: the name of the archived log that contains `OutOfMemoryError`.
For 4, meet **ripgrep**: `rg` is grep's fast cousin that searches whole folders by default, and `rg -l PATTERN DIR` lists only the matching files. Seniors reach for it all day.

checks.name: errors.txt counts error lines, any case
checks.fail: `~/answers/errors.txt` does not hold the number of lines mentioning error in any case.

checks.name: not-health.txt counts the other requests
checks.fail: `~/answers/not-health.txt` does not hold the number of requests that are not `/healthz`.

checks.name: timeouts.log has the timeout lines without retries
checks.fail: `~/answers/timeouts.log` should hold the matching lines of `app.log`, in order.

checks.name: oom.txt names the archived log
checks.fail: `~/answers/oom.txt` should hold the name of the one archived file that mentions `OutOfMemoryError`.

hints: `grep -c` counts matching lines, `-i` ignores case, `-v` keeps the lines that do **not** match. They combine: `grep -ci error file`.
Two greps in a row filter twice: `grep -i timeout app.log | grep -v retrying > ~/answers/timeouts.log`.
`rg -l OutOfMemoryError ~/logs/archive` prints the matching file (with its path; the name alone or the path both count).
steps.explain: `-c`, `-i` and `-v` turn grep from "show me" into "count me" and "everything except". `rg` does the same with sane defaults: recursive, skips `.gitignore`d and binary files, and is much faster on big trees.

steps.title: uniq -c | sort -rn (and jq)
prompt: The classic **top N** pipeline, on real data in `~/logs`. Write each answer into `~/answers/`:
1. `top-paths.txt`: the 5 most requested paths in `access.log` with their counts, biggest first, as `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5` prints them. The path is field 6 when you split on spaces.
2. `statuses.txt`: every status code (field 8) with its count, biggest first.
3. `top-failer.txt`: just the name of the user with the most `login_failed` events in `events.jsonl`, one JSON object per line.
For 3, meet **jq**, the JSON tool: `jq -r '.user' file` prints one field of every line, and `jq -r 'select(.event == "login_failed") | .user' file` prints it only for matching lines.

checks.name: top-paths.txt is the top 5 paths with counts
checks.fail: `~/answers/top-paths.txt` should be the five most requested paths (field 6), each with its count, biggest first.

checks.name: statuses.txt counts every status code, biggest first
checks.fail: `~/answers/statuses.txt` should list every status code (field 8) with its count, biggest first.

checks.name: top-failer.txt names the user with the most failed logins
checks.fail: `~/answers/top-failer.txt` should hold just one user name: the one with the most `login_failed` events.

hints: `cut -d' ' -f6 access.log` (or `awk '{print $6}'`) prints just the paths. `uniq -c` counts runs of identical lines, so `sort` first.
Biggest first is `sort -rn` (numeric, reversed); `head -5` keeps five.
For the user: the jq `select(...)` above, then the same `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1`, and `awk '{print $2}'` to keep just the name.
solution: cut -d' ' -f6 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5 > ~/answers/top-paths.txt
jq -r 'select(.event == "login_failed") | .user' events.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1 | awk '{print $2}' > ~/answers/top-failer.txt
steps.explain: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` answers most "who or what is the most..." questions in seconds: top paths, top IPs, top errors. `jq` slots into the same pipeline whenever the log is JSON.

steps.title: Mission: pipes and plumbing
prompt: Same tools, a story to go with them. In the mission **Pipes and plumbing**, answer **The nation's favourite**: which biscuit flavour appears in the most orders? Your new `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` pipeline is exactly the tool.
steps.explain: Pull out the field, sort, count, sort by count: once this recipe is in your fingers, most "what is the most..." questions take one line.
